# Shai Gilgeous-Alexander

| Born | July 12, 1998 Toronto, Ontario, Canada | 

**Shaivonte Aician Gilgeous-Alexander** (/ˈʃeɪ/ *SHAY*;<sup>[1]</sup> born July 12, 1998), also known by his initials **SGA**, is a Canadian professional basketball player for the Oklahoma City Thunder of the National Basketball Association (NBA). He is a four-time NBA All-Star, a four-time All-NBA First Team member, and two-time NBA Most Valuable Player (MVP). Gilgeous-Alexander led the Thunder to their first NBA championship since relocating from Seattle to Oklahoma City and was named Finals MVP.

Gilgeous-Alexander played one season of college basketball for the Kentucky Wildcats. He was selected 11th overall by the Charlotte Hornets in the first round of the 2018 NBA draft before being traded to the Los Angeles Clippers on draft night. Following his rookie season, he was traded to the Thunder in July 2019.

In the 2022–23 NBA season Gilgeous-Alexander was named to his first NBA All-Star Game and was voted to the All-NBA First Team, while finishing fourth in the league in scoring with 31.4 points per game. In the 2023–24 NBA season he finished second in MVP voting and third in the league in scoring with 30.1 points per game. In the 2024–25 NBA season, Gilgeous-Alexander won the NBA MVP award after leading the league in scoring with an average of 32.7 points per game. He later won the NBA Finals MVP award as the Thunder won the 2025 NBA Finals, becoming the fourth player in NBA history to win the MVP award, Finals MVP award, and scoring title all in the same season. In the 2025–26 NBA season he won his second league MVP award while finishing second in the league in scoring averaging 31.1 points per game.<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

With the Canada men's national basketball team, Gilgeous-Alexander won the bronze medal at the 2023 FIBA Basketball World Cup and was named to the All-Tournament Team. In 2023 and 2025 he received the Northern Star Award as Canada's Athlete of the Year. Gilgeous-Alexander was awarded Sports Illustrated Sportsperson of the Year in 2025.<sup>[5]</sup><sup>[6]</sup>

## Early life

Gilgeous-Alexander was born on July 12, 1998, in Toronto, Ontario, and grew up in nearby Hamilton.<sup>[7]</sup> His mother, Charmaine Gilgeous, is a former professional track athlete who competed in the women's 400 metres for Antigua and Barbuda at the 1992 Summer Olympics.<sup>[8]</sup> His father, Vaughn Alexander, also of Antiguan descent, played high school basketball and won a Toronto city championship while attending Georges Vanier Secondary School in the early 1990s.<sup>[9]</sup> Gilgeous-Alexander's father coached him during his youth.<sup>[10]</sup> He began high school in Hamilton at St. Thomas More Catholic Secondary School before transferring to nearby Sir Allan MacNab Secondary School. He later moved to the United States and attended Hamilton Heights Christian Academy in Chattanooga, Tennessee, for his junior and senior years to improve his basketball skills, graduating in 2017.<sup>[11]</sup><sup>[12]</sup>

## High school career

Gilgeous-Alexander initially attended St. Thomas More Catholic Secondary School in Hamilton, Ontario. In ninth grade, he did not make the school's junior team and subsequently played on the midget squad,<sup>[13]</sup> where he was named team MVP and led St. Thomas More to the midget boys' city championship.<sup>[9]</sup> Gilgeous-Alexander then transferred to nearby Sir Allan MacNab Secondary School before relocating to the United States in 2015 to attend Hamilton Heights Christian Academy in Chattanooga, Tennessee.<sup>[14]</sup> "I just thought I needed to play better competition," he said. In his senior season, Gilgeous-Alexander averaged 18.4 points, 4.4 rebounds, and 4.0 assists per game.<sup>[15]</sup>

In early 2016, he participated in the Basketball Without Borders development camp.<sup>[16]</sup>

A four-star recruit according to ESPN, Gilgeous-Alexander verbally committed to play college basketball for the Florida Gators in November 2015 before decommitting in October 2016.<sup>[17]</sup> His final five schools were Kansas, Kentucky, Syracuse, Texas, and UNLV.<sup>[15]</sup> The following month, Gilgeous-Alexander announced his decision to play for the Kentucky Wildcats after signing his national letter of intent on November 14, 2016.<sup>[17]</sup> He participated in the 2017 Kentucky Derby Festival Basketball Classic and was named the Most Valuable Player (MVP).<sup>[18]</sup> At the 2017 Nike Hoop Summit, Gilgeous-Alexander represented the World Select Team and scored 11 points in 21 minutes of play.<sup>[19]</sup>

## College career

Gilgeous-Alexander started the 2017–18 season with the Kentucky Wildcats as a reserve, sitting behind freshman point guard Quade Green, but still averaged over 30 minutes per game. After a loss to UCLA, Alexander recorded 24 points, five rebounds, and four assists against Louisville on December 29, 2017.<sup>[20]</sup> When he first stepped on the University of Kentucky's campus, Gilgeous-Alexander had long hair. However, he cut his hair early in the season and some say this started his progression from sixth man to starting point guard.<sup>[21]</sup> He continued to lead the team for the following two games, scoring 21 points against Georgia and 18 against LSU. He was a consistent contributor to a "struggling" Kentucky team that had a four-game losing streak during the season. He became a starter along with four other freshmen: Hamidou Diallo, Nick Richards, Kevin Knox II, and P. J. Washington. Despite their losses, his PPG shot up to 12.9 along with 3.8 rebounds and 4.6 assists. Gilgeous-Alexander had a great SEC tournament, earning Most Valuable Player (MVP) honours, and continued that momentum into the NCAA tournament. After playing great basketball in the first two rounds against Davidson and Buffalo, Kentucky lost to Kansas State in the Sweet 16. Gilgeous-Alexander's final college basketball moment was a missed three-point attempt at the buzzer. He concluded his freshman season and, consequently, his college career, having played 37 games with 24 starts, averaging 14.4 points, 4.1 rebounds, and 5.1 assists per game while shooting 48.5 percent from the field.<sup>[22]</sup> After the 2017–18 season, Gilgeous-Alexander declared for the 2018 NBA draft on April 9, 2018.<sup>[23]</sup>

## Professional career

### Los Angeles Clippers (2018–2019)

Gilgeous-Alexander was selected 11th overall by the Charlotte Hornets in the first round of the 2018 NBA draft on June 21, 2018. On draft night, he was traded to the Los Angeles Clippers in exchange for the 12th overall pick, Miles Bridges, and two future second-round picks.<sup>[24]</sup>

Gilgeous-Alexander participated in the 2018 NBA Summer League with the Los Angeles Clippers in the Las Vegas Summer League. Starting all four of his games, he averaged 19.0 points, 4.8 rebounds, and 4.0 assists per game while shooting 45.8 percent from the field.<sup>[25]</sup><sup>[26]</sup><sup>[27]</sup> With this performance, Gilgeous-Alexander became the first player in Las Vegas Summer League history to average at least 19.0 points, 4.0 assists, and 2.0 steals over a minimum of three appearances.<sup>[28]</sup>

Gilgeous-Alexander scored a season-best 24 points in a 131–127 loss to the Portland Trail Blazers on December 17, 2018.<sup>[29]</sup> He later matched this scoring mark on January 18, 2019, scoring 24 points in a 112–94 loss to the Golden State Warriors.<sup>[30]</sup> Eleven days later, on January 29, he was selected for the World Team representing Canada in the 2019 Rising Stars Challenge.<sup>[31]</sup> Gilgeous-Alexander finished his rookie season with an appearance in the 2019 NBA playoffs, where the Clippers were eliminated by the Golden State Warriors in six games during the Western Conference First Round. In Game 4 of the series on April 21, he recorded a then-career-high 25 points in a 113–105 loss to the Warriors.<sup>[32]</sup>

### Oklahoma City Thunder (2019–present)

#### 2019–20: Improving as a sophomore

The Los Angeles Clippers traded Gilgeous-Alexander along with Danilo Gallinari, five first-round draft picks, and the rights to swap two other first-round picks to the Oklahoma City Thunder in exchange for NBA All-Star Paul George on July 10, 2019.<sup>[33]</sup> On October 8, Gilgeous-Alexander made his preseason debut with the Thunder against the Dallas Mavericks, recording 24 points and four rebounds in a 119–104 win. On December 22, Gilgeous-Alexander scored a then-career-high 32 points with five assists, three rebounds, and two steals in a 118–112 win over the Los Angeles Clippers.<sup>[34]</sup> On January 13, 2020, Gilgeous-Alexander recorded his first career triple-double with 20 points, 10 assists, and a career-high 20 rebounds in a 117–104 win over the Minnesota Timberwolves. With this performance, he became the second player after Russell Westbrook to record a 20–20–10 statline in the last 30 years and the youngest ever to achieve it.<sup>[35]</sup><sup>[36]</sup>

#### 2020–22: Breakthrough and injuries

On December 26, 2020, Gilgeous-Alexander put up 24 points, seven rebounds, nine assists, and a game-winning jump shot in a 109–107 win against the Charlotte Hornets.<sup>[37]</sup> On February 24, 2021, Gilgeous-Alexander scored a then-career-high 42 points to give the Thunder a 102–99 win over the San Antonio Spurs.<sup>[38]</sup> On March 24, after playing 35 games, his season ended due to a tear in his plantar fascia.<sup>[39]</sup>

On August 3, 2021, Gilgeous-Alexander and the Thunder agreed to a five-year, $172 million rookie extension.<sup>[40]</sup>

On December 18, 2021, Gilgeous-Alexander scored 18 points and made a game-winning three-pointer at the buzzer to lift the Thunder over his former team, the Los Angeles Clippers, 104–103.<sup>[41]</sup> Four days later, he recorded his second career triple-double, with 27 points, 11 rebounds and 12 assists, in a 108–94 victory over the Denver Nuggets.<sup>[42]</sup> On December 27, Gilgeous-Alexander was named the NBA Western Conference Player of the Week for Week 10 (December 20–26), his first career NBA Player of the Week award. He led the Thunder to a 3–1 week with averages of 27.5 points, 6.3 rebounds and 7.0 assists.<sup>[43]</sup> On March 28, 2022, Gilgeous-Alexander was ruled out for the rest of the season with an ankle injury.<sup>[44]</sup> He finished the season with then-career highs of 24.5 points and 5.9 assists per game.<sup>[44]</sup>

#### 2022–23: First All-Star and All-NBA First Team selection

On October 31, 2022, Gilgeous-Alexander was named the NBA Western Conference Player of the Week for Week 2 (October 24–30), his second career NBA Player of the Week award. He led the Thunder to an undefeated 3–0 week with averages of 31.7 points, 5.3 rebounds, and 7.7 assists.<sup>[45]</sup> On November 16, Gilgeous-Alexander tied a then-career-high with 42 points, alongside a game-winning three-pointer, six rebounds and seven assists, in a 121–120 win over the Washington Wizards.<sup>[46]</sup> On December 19, Gilgeous-Alexander put up 35 points alongside a buzzer-beating game-winner in a 123–121 win over the Portland Trail Blazers.<sup>[47]</sup>

On February 2, 2023, Gilgeous-Alexander was named to his first-ever NBA All-Star Game as a reserve guard for the Western Conference.<sup>[48]</sup> On February 4, he recorded 42 points, four rebounds, six assists, three steals, and two blocks in a 153–121 win over the Houston Rockets.<sup>[49]</sup> On February 10, Gilgeous-Alexander recorded a then-career-high 44 points on 13-of-16 shooting from the field and 18-of-19 shooting from the free throw line in a 138–129 win over the Trail Blazers. He became the first player in Thunder history to score 40-plus points on 80 percent from the field.<sup>[50]</sup> Gilgeous-Alexander ended the season with a then-career-high 31.4 points per game, joining Kevin Durant and Russell Westbrook as the only players in Thunder history to average at least 30 points per game in a season.<sup>[51]</sup> Gilgeous-Alexander became the second guard in NBA history behind Michael Jordan to average at least 30 points, four rebounds, four assists, one steal, and one block while shooting at least 50 percent from the field. He subsequently became the youngest guard in NBA history to average 30 points on 50 percent from the field, beating Jordan's record.<sup>[52]</sup><sup>[53]</sup> On May 2, Gilgeous-Alexander finished fifth in voting for the NBA Most Valuable Player (MVP).<sup>[54]</sup> He was also named to his first All-NBA First Team.<sup>[55]</sup>

#### 2023–24: MVP runner-up and best Western Conference record

On November 8, 2023, Gilgeous-Alexander scored 43 points on 15-of-22 shooting from the field and 12-of-13 from the free throw line in a 128–120 win over the Cleveland Cavaliers.<sup>[56]</sup> On November 14, Gilgeous-Alexander put up 28 points and a career-high seven steals in a 123–87 win over the San Antonio Spurs. He also had his fifth straight game with 25 points on 55 percent from the field, the longest such streak in Thunder franchise history.<sup>[57]</sup> On November 18, Gilgeous-Alexander recorded 40 points, seven rebounds, six assists, two steals and two blocks in a 130–123 overtime win over the Golden State Warriors.<sup>[58]</sup> On December 16, Gilgeous-Alexander put up 25 points, six rebounds, eight assists, two steals, and a game-winning mid-range jump shot in a 118–117 win over the Denver Nuggets.<sup>[59]</sup> On January 25, 2024, Gilgeous-Alexander was named a Western Conference starter for the 2024 NBA All-Star Game, marking his second consecutive selection and his first selection as a starter.<sup>[60]</sup> On March 12, Gilgeous-Alexander recorded 30 points, 10 rebounds, and five assists in a 121–111 loss to the Indiana Pacers. This marked his 48th 30-point game of the season, surpassing Kevin Durant's previous Thunder franchise record of 47 for the most 30-point games in a season.<sup>[61]</sup> Gilgeous-Alexander finished second in MVP voting and was selected to the All-NBA First Team for the second consecutive season. Led by his play, the Thunder won 57 games and entered the 2024 NBA playoffs as the Western Conference's top seed, their first time doing so since 2013.<sup>[62]</sup><sup>[63]</sup>

In the playoffs, the Thunder swept the New Orleans Pelicans in four games in the Western Conference First Round to advance to the Western Conference Semifinals, the franchise's first appearance there since 2016. Gilgeous-Alexander finished Game 4 with 24 points and 10 rebounds.<sup>[64]</sup> The Thunder lost to the Dallas Mavericks in six games despite Gilgeous-Alexander's then-playoff career-high 36 points, along with eight assists, two blocks, and zero turnovers in the 117–116 close-out loss in Game 6.<sup>[65]</sup>

#### 2024–25: MVP season, scoring title, NBA championship, and Finals MVP

On November 11, 2024, Gilgeous-Alexander scored a then-career-high 45 points, along with three rebounds, nine assists, five steals and two blocks in a 134–128 win over his former team, the Los Angeles Clippers.<sup>[66]</sup> On December 26, Gilgeous-Alexander tied his then-career-high with 45 points on 15-of-22 shooting, 4-of-5 from three, 11-of-11 from the free throw line, along with seven rebounds, eight assists, one steal and two blocks in a 120–114 win over the Indiana Pacers.<sup>[67]</sup> During the month of December, Gilgeous-Alexander led the Thunder to a 12–1 record while averaging an NBA-best 33.3 points on 56.3 percent from the field to go along with 5.8 rebounds, 5.2 assists, 2.5 steals, and 1.2 blocks per game. He captured Player of the Month honours in back-to-back months for November and December.<sup>[68]</sup>

On January 2, 2025, Gilgeous-Alexander led the Thunder to their 13th straight win, setting a new franchise record for most consecutive regular-season wins in the franchise's Oklahoma City era.<sup>[69]</sup> On January 5, Gilgeous-Alexander recorded 33 points, 11 rebounds, six assists, three steals, and two blocks in a 105–92 win over the Boston Celtics. The victory marked the team's franchise-record 15th consecutive regular-season win. The previous record of 14 games had been set by the 1995–96 Seattle SuperSonics from February to March 1996.<sup>[70]</sup><sup>[71]</sup> On January 22, Gilgeous-Alexander recorded a career-high 54 points, eight rebounds, five assists, three steals, and two blocks in a 123–114 win over the Utah Jazz.<sup>[72]</sup> On January 25, Gilgeous-Alexander was named a Western Conference starter for the 2025 NBA All-Star Game, marking his third consecutive selection and his second selection in a row as a starter.<sup>[73]</sup> On January 29, Gilgeous-Alexander scored 52 points in a 116–109 loss against the Golden State Warriors.<sup>[74]</sup> On February 5, Gilgeous-Alexander scored 50 points along with eight rebounds, five assists, two steals, and one block in a 140–109 win over the Phoenix Suns. He became the ninth player in NBA history to score at least 50 points three times in a seven-game span.<sup>[75]</sup><sup>[76]</sup>

On March 3, Gilgeous-Alexander scored 51 points, along with seven assists, five rebounds, one steal, and one block in a 137–128 win over the Houston Rockets. It was his fourth outing with at least 50 points that season. He tied Kevin Durant for second in franchise history, trailing only Russell Westbrook, who had five 50-point games while with the team. Gilgeous-Alexander also became just the 12th player in NBA history to achieve four (or more) games with at least 50 points in a single season.<sup>[77]</sup><sup>[78]</sup> On March 12, Gilgeous-Alexander recorded 34 points, five rebounds, and seven assists in a 118–112 win over the Boston Celtics. He also became the fastest player in Thunder franchise history to achieve 10,000 career points, doing so in 368 games and surpassing the previous record set by Kevin Durant at 381 games.<sup>[79]</sup> On March 25, Gilgeous-Alexander recorded 32 points, seven rebounds, and five assists in a 121–105 win over the Sacramento Kings. The performance marked his 65th consecutive game scoring 20 or more points, surpassing Kevin Durant's Thunder franchise record of 64 such games.<sup>[80]</sup>

Gilgeous-Alexander finished the regular season as the first Canadian to lead the NBA in scoring and the third international player to achieve the feat. He finished the season with the most 20-point games (75), 30-point games (49), 40-point games (13) and 50-point games (4). His streak of 72 consecutive games scoring at least 20 points became the longest such streak since the 1960s, following Wilt Chamberlain (80 games), and Oscar Robertson (76 games).<sup>[81]</sup> It was also Gilgeous-Alexander's third consecutive season averaging at least 30 points, joining a list occupied by Michael Jordan, Wilt Chamberlain, Oscar Robertson, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, James Harden and Bob McAdoo.<sup>[82]</sup> He was named the NBA Most Valuable Player (MVP) for the 2024–25 NBA season, becoming just the second Canadian to win the award, following Steve Nash who first claimed it in back-to-back seasons in 2005 and 2006. Gilgeous-Alexander also led the Thunder to the best record in franchise history at 68–14, tied for the fifth-best regular season record in NBA history.<sup>[83]</sup>

In the playoffs, the Thunder swept the Memphis Grizzlies in four games in the Western Conference First Round to advance to the Western Conference Semifinals. On April 26, Gilgeous-Alexander scored a then-playoff career-high 38 points in Game 4, completing the four-game sweep in a 117–115 win over the Grizzlies.<sup>[84]</sup> In Game 7 of the Western Conference Semifinals against the Denver Nuggets, Gilgeous-Alexander recorded 35 points, three rebounds, four assists, and three steals in a 125–93 win, securing his first Western Conference Finals appearance. He became the sixth player in NBA playoff history to record 35+ points and 0 turnovers in a Game 7.<sup>[85]</sup> In Game 2 of the Western Conference Finals, Gilgeous-Alexander tied his then-playoff career-high with 38 points and added eight assists in a 118–103 victory over the Minnesota Timberwolves, leading the Thunder to a 2–0 series lead. With this performance, he became the first player in franchise history to record five consecutive 30-point games in the playoffs.<sup>[86]</sup> On May 26, in Game 4 of the Western Conference Finals, Gilgeous-Alexander recorded a then playoff career-high 40 points, along with nine rebounds and 10 assists, narrowly missing a triple-double, as the Thunder secured a 128–126 victory over the Timberwolves to take a 3–1 series lead.<sup>[87]</sup> After the Thunder won the series in five games, Gilgeous-Alexander was named the unanimous winner of the Western Conference Finals MVP. He averaged 31.4 points, 5.2 rebounds, 8.2 assists, and 1.8 steals per game en route to his first NBA Finals appearance and the Thunder's first since 2012. Gilgeous-Alexander also recorded his 10th 30-point, five-assist statline, making him one of only three players in NBA history to accomplish this feat at least 10 times in a single playoff run. The other two players to achieve this are Michael Jordan and LeBron James.<sup>[88]</sup>

In Game 1 of the 2025 NBA Finals, Gilgeous-Alexander scored a game-high 38 points in a narrow 111–110 loss to the Indiana Pacers. His 38 points marked the third-most scored in an NBA Finals debut, behind only Allen Iverson's 48 points in 2001 and George Mikan's 42 points in 1949.<sup>[89]</sup> In Game 2, he followed up with 34 points in a 123–107 victory over the Pacers. His first basket of the game made him the 12th player in NBA history to reach 3,000 combined points in the regular season and playoffs.<sup>[90]</sup> His 72 combined points across the first two games set a record for the most by any player in their first two Finals games, surpassing Iverson's previous mark of 71 points from 2001.<sup>[91]</sup><sup>[92]</sup> In Game 5, Gilgeous-Alexander recorded 31 points, 10 assists, and four blocks in a 120–109 victory that gave the Thunder a 3–2 series lead. With this performance, he recorded his 12th postseason game with at least 30 points and 5 assists, setting a new NBA record for the most such games in a single playoff run. He surpassed the previous mark of 11, held jointly by Michael Jordan and LeBron James. Gilgeous-Alexander also became one of only four NBA players to have 15 or more 30-point games in a single postseason run. The other three players on that list are Michael Jordan (1992), Hakeem Olajuwon (1995), and Kobe Bryant (2009).<sup>[93]</sup> The Thunder defeated the Pacers 103–91 in Game 7 to win the series 4–3, with Gilgeous-Alexander named NBA Finals MVP, becoming the first Canadian to earn the honor.<sup>[94]</sup> He became the fourth player in NBA history, after Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Michael Jordan, and Shaquille O'Neal, to achieve the distinction of winning the MVP award, Finals MVP award, and scoring title all in the same season.<sup>[95]</sup>

#### 2025–26: Back-to-back MVPs and Clutch Player of the Year

Gilgeous-Alexander agreed to a record four-year, $285 million extension with the Thunder on July 1, 2025.<sup>[96]</sup> He began the 2025–26 season with record-breaking performances. In the season opener against the Houston Rockets on October 21, Gilgeous-Alexander scored 35 points and made a pair of game-winning free throws in a 125–124 double-overtime victory.<sup>[97]</sup> In the following game, a rematch of the 2025 NBA Finals against the Indiana Pacers on October 23, he recorded career highs of 55 points and 23 free throws made out of 26 attempted, while adding eight rebounds, five assists, and two steals in a 141–135 double-overtime win. This made the Thunder the first team in NBA history to play double overtime in the first two games of a season. His 55 points were the third-highest in franchise history since the team's relocation from Seattle to Oklahoma City in 2008, and tied Russell Westbrook for the most 50-point games in franchise history with five. Across these two games, his combined 40 free throw attempts set an NBA record for most attempts through the first two games of a season, while his combined 90 points ranked fifth most in NBA history through the first two games of a season, trailing only Wilt Chamberlain, Anthony Davis, and Michael Jordan.<sup>[98]</sup><sup>[99]</sup><sup>[100]</sup>

Gilgeous-Alexander recorded a double-double with 30 points and 12 assists in a 126–107 victory over the Los Angeles Clippers on November 4. This performance marked his 80th consecutive game scoring 20 or more points, surpassing Oscar Robertson’s streak to become the third-longest in NBA history.<sup>[101]</sup> It also contributed to the Thunder's franchise record for the longest season-opening winning streak of 8–0.<sup>[102]</sup> On November 30, Gilgeous-Alexander scored 26 points in a 123–115 win over the Portland Trail Blazers. On December 10, Gilgeous-Alexander led the Thunder to the longest winning streak in franchise history at 16 games, following a 138–89 win over the Phoenix Suns, while guiding the team to a 24–1 record, tying the best start to a regular season in NBA history alongside the 2015–16 Golden State Warriors. The Thunder also posted the largest scoring differential through 25 games ever at +17.5 points per game. On December 13, the historic streak came to an end in a narrow 111–109 loss to the San Antonio Spurs.<sup>[103]</sup><sup>[104]</sup> On December 22, Gilgeous-Alexander recorded 31 points, 10 rebounds, and eight assists in a 119–103 victory over the Memphis Grizzlies. It was his 100th consecutive 20-point game, joining Wilt Chamberlain as the only players to achieve such a feat in NBA history.<sup>[105]</sup><sup>[106]</sup> On January 2, 2026, Gilgeous-Alexander was named Western Conference Player of the Month for games played in December after he led the Thunder to a 9–4 record, averaging 31.4 points, 4.6 rebounds, and 6.1 assists per game while shooting 59.4 percent from the field. It was his fifth career Player of the Month honours.<sup>[107]</sup><sup>[108]</sup>

On January 7, 2026, Gilgeous-Alexander hit a mid-range jumper at the buzzer to force overtime against the Utah Jazz. He finished the game with 46 points, six rebounds, and six assists, leading the Thunder to a 129–125 overtime victory.<sup>[109]</sup><sup>[110]</sup> On January 21, Gilgeous-Alexander recorded 40 points, seven rebounds, and 11 assists on 16-of-19 shooting in a 122–102 win over the Milwaukee Bucks. In the process, he joined Chamberlain (three times) as the only players in NBA history to record 40+ points, 10+ assists, and 5+ rebounds on at least 80% shooting from the field in a game.<sup>[111]</sup> On March 9, Gilgeous-Alexander recorded 35 points, nine rebounds, and a career-high 15 assists, and hit a game-winning three-pointer, in a 129–126 win over the Denver Nuggets. Three days later, he scored 35 points in a 104–102 win over the Boston Celtics. With these performances, he broke Wilt Chamberlain's record for the most consecutive 20-point games.<sup>[112]</sup><sup>[113]</sup> For the regular season, Gilgeous-Alexander won his second consecutive NBA Most Valuable Player (MVP) award, becoming the 14th player in NBA history to win the award in back-to-back years, and also earned his first-ever NBA Clutch Player of the Year award.<sup>[114]</sup><sup>[115]</sup> He also became the first guard in NBA history to average at least 30 points on at least 55% shooting from the field in a season.<sup>[116]</sup>

Oklahoma City went into the 2026 NBA playoffs as 1st seed in the Western Conference. In the first round, they swept the Phoenix Suns, and in Game 3, Gilgeous-Alexander put up a playoff career-high 42 points on 15-of-18 shooting, along with eight assists. He became only the second NBA player to score 40 or more points on at least 83.3% shooting in a playoff game.<sup>[117]</sup><sup>[118]</sup> The Thunder then swept the Los Angeles Lakers in the Western Conference Semifinals. In Game 4, Gilgeous-Alexander recorded 35 points and eight assists to lead the Thunder to a 115–110 win, making them the 11th team to sweep the first two rounds of the NBA Playoffs. The game marked his 26th 30-point playoff game in his Thunder career, tying Russell Westbrook for second-most in franchise history.<sup>[119]</sup><sup>[120]</sup> Gilgeous-Alexander and the Thunder were eliminated by the San Antonio Spurs in seven games in the Western Conference Finals. In the decisive Game 7, Gilgeous-Alexander recorded a game-high 35 points and a game-high 9 assists in a 111–103 loss.<sup>[121]</sup><sup>[122]</sup>

On October 22, 2026, Gilgeous-Alexander put up 17 points on 6-of-19 shooting from the field in a 96–84 win over the Denver Nuggets. His record for the most consecutive 20-point games in NBA history ended at 141 games.<sup>[123]</sup><sup>[124]</sup>

## National team career

Gilgeous-Alexander represented the Canada men's junior national basketball team at the 2016 FIBA Americas Under-18 Championship in Valdivia, Chile. He played in all five games of the tournament, averaging 7.8 points, 4.0 rebounds, and 5.4 assists per game while shooting 39.4 percent from the field.<sup>[125]</sup> The team won the silver medal following a 99–84 loss to the United States in the final. Later that year, Gilgeous-Alexander joined the senior men's national basketball team for the 2016 FIBA World Olympic Qualifying Tournament in Manila, Philippines.<sup>[126]</sup> Canada lost to France in the final and failed to qualify for the 2016 Summer Olympics.<sup>[127]</sup>

Gilgeous-Alexander was one of 14 players to agree to a three-year commitment to play with the national team on May 24, 2022, aiming to break a decades-long trend of failing to qualify for the Olympic basketball tournament.<sup>[128]</sup> At the 2023 FIBA Basketball World Cup, Gilgeous-Alexander was the central figure on the Canadian roster, leading them on a historic deep run.<sup>[129]</sup><sup>[130]</sup> They qualified to the quarter-finals of the tournament on September 3, in the process securing a berth at the 2024 Summer Olympics, which he called "almost indescribable."<sup>[131]</sup> The team ultimately won the bronze medal after defeating the United States in the third-place game. This was Canada's first ever World Cup medal, and first medal at a major global tournament since the 1936 Summer Olympics.<sup>[132]</sup><sup>[133]</sup> In recognition of his individual play, Gilgeous-Alexander was named to the All-Tournament Team.<sup>[134]</sup> For both this and his feats in the NBA in 2023, he received the Northern Star Award as Canada's Athlete of the Year and the Lionel Conacher Award as the Canadian Press' choice for Canadian Male Athlete of the Year. Gilgeous-Alexander was only the second basketball player to receive the two honours, in both cases after Steve Nash. He would again receive the honour in 2025.<sup>[135]</sup><sup>[136]</sup>

Gilgeous-Alexander was named to Canada's roster for the 2024 Summer Olympics in Paris.<sup>[137]</sup> After a strong unbeaten performance in the group stage, which was deemed the "group of death" by experts,<sup>[138]</sup><sup>[139]</sup> Canada was surprisingly eliminated in the quarterfinals by hosts France.<sup>[140]</sup> Gilgeous-Alexander was named to the tournament's All-Second Team after averaging 21.0 points, 4.3 rebounds, and 4.0 assists per game.<sup>[141]</sup>

## Player profile

Listed at 6 feet 6 inches (1.98 m) tall and weighing 195 pounds (88.5 kg), Gilgeous-Alexander is a combo guard known for his ability to slash through defenses and score on all three levels. His 6-foot 11 inch (2.11 m) wingspan, body control, speed, and embrace of defensive contact make him one of the best slashers in the history of the NBA, boasting a 68 percent career field goal percentage within three feet of the basket.<sup>[142]</sup>

Gilgeous-Alexander is regarded as a two-way player: he earned All-Defensive Team votes from 2023 to 2026 and placed 7th in the voting for the 2024 Defensive Player of the Year Award.<sup>[143]</sup>

Gilgeous-Alexander has earned widespread praise across the NBA for his leadership, work ethic, and maturity. Former teammates Patrick Beverley and Chris Paul recognized his relentless work ethic and dedication to the game from beginning of his career, with Beverley comparing Gilgeous-Alexander's mindset to the likes of Kobe Bryant and Michael Jordan.<sup>[144]</sup><sup>[145]</sup> Thunder head coach Mark Daigneault has praised Gilgeous-Alexander for his composure and selflessness, highlighting how he leads by example on and off the court.<sup>[146]</sup>

Gilgeous-Alexander has faced heavy fan criticism on social media for his high free throw numbers and tendency to embellish contact when driving. He led the NBA in total free throws made from the 2022–23 season to the 2024–25 season, though he has never led in free throws attempted. Former NBA player Richard Jefferson addressed the narrative of Gilgeous-Alexander being a "free-throw merchant" to discredit his offensive prowess, saying, "Shai is one of the most impressive people that I've ever talked to. I asked him about the free throws, and he's like, 'Yeah. You know what's crazy about it is that two years ago, I averaged almost 11 free throws a game but we finished 10th and no one cared. When I wasn't sending their best favorite player home when I wasn't sending their team home, then no one cared that I was shooting 11 free throws a night and scoring this amount of points.' To me, this is the type of sickos that we love."<sup>[147]</sup>

## Endorsements

Gilgeous-Alexander signed an endorsement deal with Converse on July 8, 2020.<sup>[149]</sup> According to the Netflix docuseries *Power Moves with Shaquille O'Neal*, O'Neal attempted to sign Gilgeous-Alexander to Reebok as his initial shoe contract was set to expire at the conclusion of the 2023–24 NBA season.<sup>[150]</sup> However, Gilgeous-Alexander ultimately re-signed with Converse on a lucrative multi-year contract extension and was named Creative Director of Converse Basketball. In this role, he had creative input across all basketball product designs and the opportunity to launch his own signature sneaker line, beginning with the SHAI 001, which was released on September 4, 2025.<sup>[151]</sup><sup>[152]</sup> On June 16, 2026, it was announced that Gilgeous-Alexander had left Converse to sign with its parent company Nike.<sup>[153]</sup>

## Legal issues

Gilgeous-Alexander purchased a lakefront property in Burlington, Ontario, in May 2023, which had previously been occupied by bankrupt cryptocurrency trader Aiden Pleterski. Within days of moving in, Gilgeous-Alexander and his partner vacated the residence due to ongoing security concerns related to Pleterski's highly publicized fraud and bankruptcy case, which had led to threats and repeated visits from investors seeking Pleterski. Gilgeous-Alexander subsequently filed a lawsuit to rescind the purchase, alleging that the seller, who had leased the property to Pleterski, failed to disclose the property's connection to the trader and the associated safety risks.<sup>[154]</sup><sup>[155]</sup> The court ruled in favour of Gilgeous-Alexander, finding fraudulent misrepresentation on the part of the seller and awarded him damages for mortgage and insurance payments incurred. Consequently, the purchase was reversed, and the seller's appeal was denied. The case set a precedent in Ontario real estate law by expanding the scope of required property disclosures to include latent safety risks beyond the physical condition of the property.<sup>[156]</sup><sup>[157]</sup>

Gilgeous-Alexander's home in Nichols Hills, Oklahoma, was burglarized while he was at the Paycom Center in downtown Oklahoma City, playing the Washington Wizards on October 30, 2025.<sup>[158]</sup>

## Personal life

Gilgeous-Alexander is of Antiguan descent.<sup>[8]</sup> He has one sibling, a younger brother named Thomasi Gilgeous-Alexander, who played college basketball for the Evansville Purple Aces<sup>[159]</sup> and Northeastern Oklahoma A&M NEO.<sup>[160]</sup> Gilgeous-Alexander's first cousin, Nickeil Alexander-Walker, is an NBA player for the Atlanta Hawks. The two share a close relationship, having lived together at their high school coach Zach Ferrell's house.<sup>[10]</sup> Gilgeous-Alexander married his high school sweetheart, Hailey Summers, on February 14, 2024.<sup>[9]</sup> Summers gave birth to their son, named Ares, on April 25, 2024.<sup>[161]</sup>

Gilgeous-Alexander is considered a hometown hero in Hamilton. On August 7, 2025, the city held "Shai Rally Day" at Hamilton Stadium to celebrate his accomplishments. Hamilton mayor Andrea Horwath presented him with the Key to the City, and they announced the installation of commemorative "Shai Gilgeous-Alexander Way" street signs along Mohawk Road, the neighbourhood where he grew up.<sup>[162]</sup> He was also honored during halftime of that day's Hamilton Tiger-Cats game, where he wore a custom #2 Tiger-Cats jersey.<sup>[163]</sup> In February 2026, Gilgeous-Alexander joined the ownership group of the TD Coliseum in his hometown of Hamilton following the arena's renovation, and the atrium is named after his son Ares with a planned mural.<sup>[164]</sup>

# Bronny James

| High school | Sierra Canyon (Los Angeles, California) | 

**LeBron Raymone** "**Bronny**" **James Jr.** (born October 6, 2004) is an American professional basketball player for the Los Angeles Lakers of the National Basketball Association (NBA). A consensus four-star recruit, James was named a McDonald's All-American as a senior in high school in 2023. He played one season of college basketball for the USC Trojans before being selected by the Lakers in the second round of the 2024 NBA draft. He is the eldest child and former teammate of LeBron James Sr., making them the first active father–son duo in NBA history.

## Early life and career

James was born on October 6, 2004, in Akron, Ohio, to reigning NBA Rookie of the Year LeBron James, age 19, and his girlfriend Savannah Brinson, age 18.<sup>[1]</sup> He was raised by both of his parents,<sup>[2]</sup> who married in 2013.<sup>[3]</sup> As a child, James played several sports including basketball and soccer, but his father did not allow him to play football or ice hockey because of safety concerns.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[5]</sup>

By the time James was 10 years old, his highlights from youth basketball games were drawing national attention.<sup>[6]</sup><sup>[7]</sup><sup>[8]</sup> During his childhood, James played for the Miami City Ballers with teammates such as Jett Howard and the Houston-based Gulf Coast Blue Chips.<sup>[9]</sup><sup>[10]</sup> In middle school, he competed for the North Coast Blue Chips, a team that included Mikey Williams.<sup>[11]</sup> James also played for Old Trail School in Bath Township, Summit County, Ohio, where he attended middle school, and led his team to an Independent School League tournament win.<sup>[12]</sup> In July 2018, a youth game featuring James was canceled after a fan wearing a Michael Jordan jersey heckled his father and was denied entrance.<sup>[13]</sup> On August 6, 2018, he enrolled at Crossroads School, a private K–12 school in Santa Monica, California.<sup>[14]</sup> California state rules prevented him from immediately joining the varsity team because he was in eighth grade.<sup>[15]</sup><sup>[16]</sup> On December 3, 2018, in his first game for the school, James scored 27 points in a 61–48 victory over Culver City Middle School.<sup>[17]</sup> In April 2019, he made his Nike Elite Youth Basketball League (EYBL) debut with Strive for Greatness.<sup>[18]</sup>

## High school career

### Freshman season

On May 29, 2019, James transferred to Sierra Canyon School, a private K–12 school in Chatsworth, Los Angeles, for his freshman year of high school. He joined the school with his brother Bryce and incoming senior Zaire Wade, son of Dwyane Wade, a longtime teammate of James’s father.<sup>[19]</sup><sup>[20]</sup> Sierra Canyon's basketball program, under head coach Andre Chevalier, was one of the best in the nation and won the previous two California Interscholastic Federation (CIF) Open Division state titles.<sup>[21]</sup> The 2019–20 team was led by five-star recruits Brandon Boston Jr. and Ziaire Williams, who transferred there for their senior years.<sup>[22]</sup> Before the season, ESPN announced that its networks would air 15 of the team's games.<sup>[23]</sup> Despite heavy media attention, James's father barred him from being interviewed.<sup>[24]</sup>

On November 21, 2019, James made his high school debut, scoring 10 points off the bench in a 91–44 win over Montgomery High School.<sup>[25]</sup> On December 14, he scored 15 points, including a go-ahead layup, and was named the game's most valuable player (MVP) in a 59–56 victory over his father's alma mater, St. Vincent–St. Mary High School.<sup>[26]</sup> On January 15, 2020, James scored a season-high 17 points in a 117–62 win over Viewpoint School.<sup>[27]</sup> Five days later, during a Hoophall Classic game against Paul VI Catholic High School, a spectator threw an orange peel at James, briefly stopping play. A clip of the incident went viral, drawing criticism from James’s father, and the spectator apologized.<sup>[28]</sup><sup>[29]</sup>

Sierra Canyon went 30–4 on the season and reached the Open Division state championship game, which was canceled due to the COVID-19 pandemic.<sup>[30]</sup> As a freshman, James averaged 4.1 points and 15 minutes per game, and was the team's only player to appear in all 34 games.<sup>[27]</sup>

### Sophomore season

On November 12, 2020, James played his first preseason game as a sophomore for California Basketball Club (CBC), a travel team representing Sierra Canyon, against Air Nado, a team affiliated with Coronado High School, at the High School Showcase. He scored nine points, all in the first half.<sup>[31]</sup> In February 2021, James tore his meniscus at practice and underwent surgery. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, he had not played any official games for Sierra Canyon in the 2020–21 season, which was set to begin later that year.<sup>[32]</sup> After missing most of the season, James returned against Centennial High School in the CIF Southern Section Open Division final on June 11. He scored seven points in an 80–72 loss.<sup>[33]</sup> Sierra Canyon, led by junior Amari Bailey, finished the season with a 16–2 record.<sup>[34]</sup>

### Junior season

In James's junior season, his Sierra Canyon team was led by seniors Amari Bailey and Kijani Wright.<sup>[35]</sup> On December 4, 2021, he scored a game-high 19 points in a 71–53 win over St. Vincent–St. Mary High School in the Chosen-1's Invitational at Staples Center, as Bailey was sidelined with an ankle injury.<sup>[36]</sup> His team was upset by Harvard-Westlake School in the CIF Southern Section Open Division semifinals, where he scored four points.<sup>[37]</sup>

Sierra Canyon reached the Open Division regional final, losing to Centennial High School, 83–59, and James was held scoreless while playing through hip soreness. The team ended the season with a 26–5 record.<sup>[38]</sup> As a junior, James averaged 8.8 points, 3.3 rebounds, 2.8 assists and 1.9 steals per game in 29 appearances.<sup>[39]</sup>

### Senior season

In his senior season, James stepped into a leading role and was joined on the team by his younger brother, Bryce.<sup>[40]</sup><sup>[41]</sup> In August 2022, he played alongside his Sierra Canyon teammates for CBC in three exhibition games in Europe. In his second game, James led all scorers with 25 points in a 97–85 loss to U18 French Select in Paris.<sup>[42]</sup> On October 29, James and his team were evacuated from a preseason game against the Hyattsville Stags, a team representing DeMatha Catholic High School, after a fight broke out in the stands and a fan reported seeing a gun. Although no firearms were found, the game was not resumed.<sup>[43]</sup>

After missing the first two regular season games with an illness, James made his senior debut on November 26, recording 13 points, four assists and three rebounds in a 63–60 overtime loss to Rancho Christian School.<sup>[44]</sup> In his first home game on November 30, he scored 25 points in a 77–61 win over Crossroads School.<sup>[45]</sup> In January 2023, James missed four games with a knee injury and scored 19 points in his return on February 1 as his team lost to Notre Dame High School, 88–61, at the Mission League semifinals.<sup>[46]</sup> Sierra Canyon was relegated from the CIF Open Division to Division I after its worst performance in the regular season and Southern Section Open Division playoffs in the tenure of Andre Chevalier.<sup>[47]</sup><sup>[48]</sup> James scored 10 points in an 80–68 season-ending loss to Notre Dame High School at the Division I regional final.<sup>[49]</sup> As a senior, he averaged 14.2 points, 5.5 rebounds, 2.4 assists and 1.8 steals per game, leading his team to a 23–11 record.<sup>[50]</sup><sup>[51]</sup> He was selected to play in the McDonald's All-American Game and was named to the United States team for the Nike Hoop Summit.<sup>[52]</sup><sup>[53]</sup> James scored 15 points, making five three-pointers which tied the record for most made three-pointers in the event ever while dishing out 4 assists and 2 steals, in a 109–106 loss at the McDonald's All-American Game and finished second in the event's dunk contest.<sup>[54]</sup><sup>[55]</sup> In the Nike Hoop Summit, he scored 11 points, 4 rebounds, a steal and a block as along with hitting the go ahead free-throws as his team won, 90–84.<sup>[56]</sup>

### Recruiting

By 2015, James was receiving scholarship offers and letters of interest from college basketball programs, according to his father, who commented, "It should be a violation. You shouldn't be recruiting 10-year-old kids."<sup>[57]</sup> In 2016, ESPN reported that James held offers from Duke and Kentucky.<sup>[58]</sup> Entering high school, analysts viewed him a high major NCAA Division I prospect.<sup>[59]</sup><sup>[60]</sup> He first appeared in recruiting rankings before his sophomore season, and 247Sports and ESPN rated him a four-star recruit and a top-30 player in the 2023 class.<sup>[61]</sup> Early in his junior season coming off a season ending injury, James fell to 52nd and 49th in rankings by 247Sports and ESPN, respectively,<sup>[62]</sup><sup>[63]</sup> and he dropped 31 spots to number 60 in rankings by Rivals in June 2022.<sup>[64]</sup> In his senior season, he rose in rankings from each service with On3 ranking James the 9th-best player in his class .<sup>[65]</sup> On January 17, 2023, the *Los Angeles Times* reported that James would decide between attending college at Ohio State, Oregon or USC.<sup>[66]</sup> On May 6, James announced his commitment to USC, with Ohio State being his other finalist.<sup>[67]</sup>

## College career

In March 2023, James was projected as a top-ten pick in the 2024 NBA draft and, according to ESPN NBA draft analyst Jonathan Givony, was seen as the most improved prospect in the country.<sup>[68]</sup>

On July 24, 2023, James collapsed during a USC practice session at the Galen Center. It was later revealed that he had suffered cardiac arrest caused by a congenital heart defect.<sup>[69]</sup><sup>[70]</sup> James was released from the hospital on July 27.<sup>[71]</sup>

Less than five months later, James made his collegiate debut for the Trojans on December 10, finishing with four points, three rebounds, two assists, two steals, and one block off the bench in an 84–79 loss against Long Beach State.<sup>[72]</sup> On December 30, James scored a career-high 15 points on 6-of-11 from the field and had three assists in a road loss against Oregon State.<sup>[73]</sup> On January 17, 2024, James played a season-high 30 minutes and recorded 11 points, five rebounds and six assists in an 82–67 loss to No. 12 Arizona.<sup>[74]</sup> James appeared in USC's final 25 games, starting six and averaging 4.8 points, 2.8 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 19.3 minutes.<sup>[75]</sup>

On April 5, 2024, James announced on Instagram that he would enter the 2024 NBA draft while maintaining his college eligibility and also enter the transfer portal.<sup>[76]</sup>

In early May 2024, James was medically cleared to be eligible for the NBA draft.<sup>[77]</sup><sup>[78]</sup> On May 28, 2024, it was reported that James had at least 10 workout invites from NBA teams but only visited a "couple" of those teams, which included the Los Angeles Lakers and Phoenix Suns.<sup>[79]</sup><sup>[80]</sup><sup>[81]</sup> He later had workouts with only those two teams.<sup>[82]</sup>

## Professional career

On June 27, 2024, James was selected by the Los Angeles Lakers with the 55th overall pick in the 2024 NBA draft. The selection paired James with his father, becoming the first-ever father–son duo to be in the NBA at the same time.<sup>[83]</sup> On July 3, he signed a contract with the Lakers.<sup>[84]</sup> He played for the Lakers in the NBA Summer League<sup>[85]</sup> and played six games during the preseason.<sup>[86]</sup>

On October 22, 2024, in the season opener against the Minnesota Timberwolves, James and his father became the first father–son duo to play together in the NBA.<sup>[87]</sup> Bronny debuted with a rebound in three minutes of play in the Lakers' 110–103 win over the Timberwolves.<sup>[88]</sup> On October 30, he scored his first NBA basket—alongside two assists and a steal—in a 134–110 loss to the Cleveland Cavaliers.<sup>[89]</sup> Throughout his rookie season, James was assigned several times to the South Bay Lakers of the NBA G League.<sup>[90]</sup> On December 12, 2024, he scored a game-high 30 points on 13-of-23 shooting in South Bay's 106–100 loss to the Valley Suns.<sup>[91]</sup> On January 24, 2025, he scored a then career-high 31 points in a 122–110 win over the Rip City Remix.<sup>[92]</sup>

On January 31, 2025, returning from the G League in a win over the Washington Wizards, James put up five points on 1–for–6 shooting, two rebounds, and two assists, playing the entire fourth quarter.<sup>[93]</sup> On March 20, James recorded his first double-digit scoring game of his NBA career, co-leading the shorthanded Lakers with 17 points on 7-of-10 shooting and five assists in a 118–89 loss to the Milwaukee Bucks.<sup>[94]</sup> On March 24, 2025, he scored a career and game-high 39 points with seven rebounds, four assists, a team-high four steals and one block in South Bay's 122–118 win over the Santa Cruz Warriors.<sup>[95]</sup> In the Lakers' regular-season finale on April 13, with the team's starters rested, James made his first career start and finished with four points in a 109–81 loss to the Portland Trail Blazers.<sup>[96]</sup>

On February 10, 2026, James had 12 points and six assists in a 136–108 loss to the San Antonio Spurs.<sup>[97]</sup> On April 18, in a first–round matchup against the Houston Rockets, James and his father became the first father–son duo to play in a playoff game together.<sup>[98]</sup>

## Player profile

James stands at 6 feet 1+1⁄2 inches (1.87 m) barefoot<sup>[99]</sup> and plays the point guard and shooting guard positions. Analysts during his high school years described shooting and defense as his main strengths, although he lacks the size of most NBA players with his skill set.<sup>[100]</sup><sup>[101]</sup> James was at his best at catch-and-shoot situations and could also shoot off movement.<sup>[100]</sup> He could defend point guards; his defensive anticipation and intensity were praised.<sup>[102]</sup> In 2023, ESPN's Givony said James was developing into one of the top perimeter defenders in his high school class.<sup>[103]</sup> Jonathan Wasserman described James as possessing a high basketball IQ and being a willing passer.<sup>[104]</sup> Although he was a reliable ball-handler, he could struggle to create separation from defenders. His driving and finishing abilities were labeled as weaknesses, although he had the strength to finish through contact.<sup>[100]</sup><sup>[37]</sup> James's playing style before entering the NBA drew comparisons to De'Anthony Melton, Lonzo Ball, Miles McBride, and Jrue Holiday.<sup>[104]</sup>

## Allegations of nepotism

James has been described as a nepo baby, with critics suggesting that his father's influence played a significant role in his opportunities.<sup>[105]</sup> After James was selected to play in the 2023 McDonald's All-American Game, recruiting analyst Dinos Trigonis raised concerns about a "smell of nepotism here that isn't good for our kids."<sup>[106]</sup> The Los Angeles Lakers faced similar allegations after their selection of James in the 2024 NBA draft, which allowed him to play on the same team as his father despite widespread concerns about his lackluster college play and readiness for the league.<sup>[107]</sup> According to ESPN analyst Bob Myers, James's agent, Rich Paul, discouraged other teams from selecting him in the draft, threatening to have him play overseas if chosen by another team.<sup>[108]</sup> ESPN reporter Adrian Wojnarowski addressed the claims of nepotism by stating that such practices are prevalent in various roles in the NBA.<sup>[109]</sup><sup>[110]</sup> James Jr's $2.2 million salary became fully guaranteed on June 29, 2026, one day before his dad announced he would be leaving the Lakers.<sup>[111]</sup>

## Personal life

James's godfather is NBA All-Star Chris Paul,<sup>[112]</sup><sup>[113]</sup> who is a close friend of his father.<sup>[114]</sup>

In 2020, James signed with esports organization FaZe Clan. Through the partnership, he was expected to stream *Fortnite* and *Call of Duty: Warzone* under the handle "FaZe Bronny."<sup>[115]</sup> In June 2021, James made his first appearance on the cover of *Sports Illustrated* alongside members of FaZe Clan, including NFL quarterback Kyler Murray.<sup>[116]</sup>

James has established a large social media following since high school.<sup>[117]</sup> In May 2019, he started an Instagram account and reached one million followers in his first day on the platform.<sup>[118]</sup> By the end of high school, James had over seven million followers on Instagram.<sup>[119]</sup>

Analysts projected James to have one of the highest-earning potentials from his name, image and likeness (NIL) among college athletes.<sup>[120]</sup> In February 2022, he filed for trademarks on variations of his name: Bronny, BJ Jr. and Bronald.<sup>[121]</sup> In high school, James signed NIL deals with Nike and Beats by Dre.<sup>[122]</sup>

### Basketball jersey number

James has worn the number 0 jersey because it is the number worn by his favorite NBA player, Russell Westbrook.<sup>[123]</sup> He has also worn the number 23 jersey in honor of his father.<sup>[16]</sup> In July 2024, James chose the number 9 jersey for his professional debut in the NBA during the 2024–25 Los Angeles Lakers season. The decision was made to honor the late musician Juice Wrld, alluding to Juice's 2017 debut EP *9 9 9*.<sup>[124]</sup>

# *NBA Street Vol. 2*

***NBA Street Vol. 2*** is a basketball video game developed by NuFX and EA Canada and published by Electronic Arts under the EA Sports BIG label. It is the sequel to *NBA Street* and the second installment in the *NBA Street* series. *NBA Street Vol. 2* was released on April 29, 2003, for the PlayStation 2, GameCube, and Xbox. Only the PlayStation 2 version was released in Japan; the GameCube version was planned for release in that region, but was cancelled. It was followed by NBA Street V3.

## Gameplay

[edit]
Like the previous game, *NBA Street Vol. 2* consists of 3-on-3 street basketball. There are 29 fully playable NBA teams from the 2002–03 NBA season in all modes once unlocked. The game also features four different modes to choose from including a Pick Up Game, NBA Challenge, Be a Legend, and Street School. The game also features several new trick moves and dunks, as well as introducing a level two "gamebreaker". Players will also earn reward points after every game that they win, which can be used to purchase many rewards such as players, jerseys, and courts. If players win a certain number of games, some rewards will be automatically unlocked.

In addition to "street legends", players can also unlock "NBA legends", including Larry Bird, Julius Erving, and others.

The game, at the time of release, was the only available game on the market in which three incarnations of Michael Jordan are playable: the 1985 Chicago Bulls Jordan, the 1996 Chicago Bulls Jordan, and the Washington Wizards Jordan. It is possible to play as a team made up of the three different Jordans.

The game also features an in-game soundtrack with tracks from artists including Nate Dogg featuring Eve, Pete Rock & CL Smooth, Erick Sermon featuring Redman, Benzino, MC Lyte, Black Sheep and a previously unreleased song from Nelly, who appears in the game as a playable character, along with the other members of the St. Lunatics.<sup>[1]</sup> It also features instrumental beats from producer Just Blaze.

A feature called Gamebreaker is included. When players fill up their gamebreaker meter, they have the option to either use a Gamebreaker One or save it for a Gamebreaker Two. Either way, once they use it, their team will earn more points and the opposing team will lose points. However, if players or the opposing team takes too long, they will lose their gamebreaker. If the opposing team saves their Gamebreaker, players they can use their Gamebreaker to cancel theirs.

### Game modes

[edit]
There are four modes in the game.

**Pick Up Game** - In this mode, players are able to play against the computer, or another user. They can also choose to turn the shot clock off.

**NBA Challenge** - In this mode players have to play against a series assigned teams in various regional courts. In NBA Challenge, players are able to unlock NBA Legends as well as courts, and reward points.

**Be a Legend** - This is the main mode in the game. In this mode, players create a baller, create a team and try to succeed by going from being a nobody to becoming the Street Legend champ. In order to do that, they have to gain a reputation by playing pick up games that are assigned on the map, which will lead to tournaments against street legends. The higher a player's reputation goes, the more competition they get. Also in this mode, players get to unlock the street legend characters, courts, jerseys, trick moves and their own created player. They will also earn a nickname based on their skills.

**Street School** - This mode teaches players how to play the game. The mentor is street ball legend Stretch Monroe, who will teach 26 lessons.

The game received positive reviews upon release.  GameRankings and Metacritic gave it a score of 90% and 90 out of 100 for the PlayStation 2 version;<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[6]</sup> 89% and 88 out of 100 for the GameCube version;<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[5]</sup> and 89% and 89 out of 100 for the Xbox version.<sup>[4]</sup><sup>[7]</sup>

BBC Sport gave the game a score of 93% and said, "The atmosphere of *NBA Street* is enhanced by an excellent soundtrack including hip-hop tracks from the likes of Nelly and Nate Dogg, plus various sound effects from the street - traffic, sirens, crowd abuse, etc."<sup>[8]</sup> *Maxim* gave it a score of eight out of ten and said, "even if you aren't a hoops fan, there's plenty of unintentional humor to appreciate: Seeing Yao Ming dunk on Bill Walton alone is worth the price of admission."<sup>[10]</sup> *The Village Voice* gave the PS2 version eight out of ten, saying, "The up-to-four-player game itself is hot to death."<sup>[9]</sup>

The **2026 World Series** (branded as the **2026 World Series presented by Capital One**) was the championship series of Major League Baseball's (MLB) 2026 season. The 122nd edition of the World Series, the best-of-seven playoff series was played between the American League (AL) champion Tampa Bay Rays and the National League (NL) champion Milwaukee Brewers. The series began on October 23 and finished on October 28, with the Brewers defeating the Rays in five games, winning their first championship in franchise history. Brewers catcher William Contreras was named the World Series MVP after batting .381 and recording 10/13 correct ABS challenges in the series. 

The Brewers and Rays both sought their first World Series championship. The Brewers swept the Los Angeles Dodgers to win their first National League pennant in franchise history, and their second pennant overall after winning in the American League in 1982. The Rays won their third American League pennant after defeating the Cleveland Guardians in six games, and their first since 2020. The Brewers had home-field advantage due to their league-best win–loss record.

The first two games featured narrow Brewers victories. In Game 1, the Brewers took an early lead and maintained it, while they overcame a four-run deficit built by the Rays in the first inning of Game 2, winning 3–2 and 5–4 respectively. In Game 3, however, the Brewers blew out the Rays, scoring 10 runs by the fifth inning and winning 10-1. Tampa Bay's lone win came from Game 4 in extra innings, with a Ben Williamson pinch-hit walk-off single in the twelfth inning for a 4-3 comeback victory. Milwaukee closed the series in Game 5, taking and maintaining another early lead to win 4–1 and clinch their first title in franchise history (and Milwaukee's second major sports championship in the 2020s, after the NBA's Bucks in 2021). Consequently, Tampa Bay suffered its third consecutive World Series, loss after 2020 and 2008.

It was the first World Series since 1980 in which both teams sought their first title. It was also the first World Series to feature the Automated Ball-Strike (ABS) System.

## Background

[edit]
This was the first postseason matchup between the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays in MLB history. This was the first World Series since 1980 in which neither team had previously won a championship.<sup>[1]</sup><sup>[2]</sup> The Brewers moved to the National League in 1998 as a result of the creation of the then-named Tampa Bay Devil Rays franchise, who were assigned to the American League.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup> The Brewers won two of three games against the Rays during the second series of the 2026 regular season.<sup>[5]</sup>

The luxury tax payroll for the Milwaukee Brewers (ranked 17th of 30, $192 million) and Tampa Bay Rays (21st, $161 million) guaranteed that the winner of the World Series would have the lowest-ranked payroll salary since the 2017 Houston Astros;<sup>[6]</sup> altogether, it was the lowest ranking combined payroll between World Series teams since 1991.<sup>[7]</sup> Due to these factors and the looming lockout due to inequality between large-market and small-market teams (among other issues),<sup>[8]</sup> this was dubbed the “Small Market World Series”.<sup>[9]</sup><sup>[10]</sup>

This was the first World Series since 2016 to not feature a team from California or Texas.<sup>[11]</sup> This was the sixth World Series in the Wild-Card era (1995–present) to feature the two best records in each league, last occurring in 2024.<sup>[12]</sup> This was the fourth World Series to feature two expansion-era teams, following 2015, 2019, and 2023.<sup>[13]</sup> Lastly, this was the second World Series where both teams had a retractable-roof or dome stadium as their home venue, with the first being 2023.<sup>[c]</sup>

### Milwaukee Brewers

[edit]
Despite trading team ace Freddy Peralta to the New York Mets and everyday third baseman Caleb Durbin to the Boston Red Sox in the off-season, the Milwaukee Brewers had another excellent regular season.<sup>[15]</sup> After a 18–16 (.529) start to the season, they lost just five games from May 8 through June 2. At the All-Star break, they led the National League Central by five games over the Chicago Cubs, as starter Jacob Misiorowski (MLB's season leader in earned run average and strikeouts) and catcher William Contreras were selected to the National League All-Star team.<sup>[16]</sup> After the break, the Brewers continued to win at a torrid pace, going 44–22 (.667) the rest of the season.<sup>[17]</sup> Along the way, they achieved many notable milestones.  On August 18, they won a game by a franchise-record 22 runs in a shutout win over the Seattle Mariners (they nearly accomplished this feat again by defeating the Cincinnati Reds 20–0 on September 11 to clinch a postseason berth).<sup>[18]</sup><sup>[19]</sup> They were the first team to finish a season among the top three MLB teams in runs scored and among the bottom three in home runs since the 1960 Chicago White Sox; they also led the league in batting average and on-base percentage, and finished second in stolen bases.<sup>[20]</sup> They also won 100 games for the first time in franchise history, finishing with a 103–59 (.636) record. It marked their fourth consecutive National League Central title, and they secured home-field advantage throughout the postseason for the second consecutive season.<sup>[21]</sup>

As the top-seeded team in the NL, the Brewers took on the fourth-seed San Diego Padres in the National League Division Series, which they won in four games. The three Brewers' wins came when they withstood a Padres ninth inning rally in Game 1,<sup>[22]</sup> a two-run walk-off by Jackson Chourio in the ninth inning against All-Star closer Mason Miller in Game 2,<sup>[23]</sup> and their first road postseason win in 12 games in the Game 4 clincher.<sup>[24]</sup> They then met the two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series (NLCS), a rematch of the 2025 NLCS, in which the Brewers were swept. In this meeting, the Brewers swept the Dodgers to clinch their first World Series berth in 44 years.<sup>[25]</sup> Six of Milwaukee’s seven postseason wins prior to the World Series featured comebacks. Entering the World Series, Milwaukee's bullpen had a 1.33 ERA in eight games, to go along with a 24.5% strikeout percentage while averaging 5 innings per game.<sup>[26]</sup>

This was the second World Series appearance for the Brewers, after losing to the St. Louis Cardinals in 1982, and it marked their first as a National League participant.<sup>[d]</sup> This was the city of Milwaukee's fourth World Series appearance, having featured in two with the Milwaukee Braves in 1957 and 1958, and now two with the Brewers. They became the second team, after the Houston Astros, to win pennants in both the American and National Leagues.<sup>[27]</sup>

### Tampa Bay Rays

[edit]
The Tampa Bay Rays played at George M. Steinbrenner Field for the 2025 season after Hurricane Milton damaged the roof of Tropicana Field, where they finished the season 77–85 (.475).<sup>[28]</sup> In their return season to the Trop and their first under new owner Patrick Zalupski, the Rays had a 21-game turnaround, finishing 98–64 (.605). The Rays battled atop the American League East standings with the New York Yankees until they took control on June 13. From this date, they were tied with the Yankees for one day on June 27, and led the division outright for the remainder of the season.<sup>[29]</sup> At the All-Star game, they sent an AL-leading five players, including third baseman Junior Caminero, starting pitchers Drew Rasmussen and Nick Martinez, closer Bryan Baker, and designated hitter Yandy Díaz.<sup>[30]</sup> The trade deadline saw them bring in former Brewers ace Freddy Peralta after a poor half-season with the New York Mets.<sup>[31]</sup> With the Rays, Peralta turned his season around, posting a 3.25 ERA, winning seven of his 13 starts, and later the ALCS MVP.<sup>[32]</sup> The Rays clinched the AL East against the Yankees in the nightcap of a doubleheader win to clinch their first division title since 2021, and their fifth in franchise history; the win also meant the Rays held home-field advantage throughout the American League postseason.<sup>[33]</sup>

Perhaps their biggest win of the season did not come on the field, but when Hillsborough County approved funding for the proposed new stadium in Tampa Bay on August 28, which put an end to relocation fears that had plagued the franchise for years.<sup>[34]</sup>

As the top seed in the American League, the Rays swept the New York Yankees in three games in the Division Series, with Drew Rasmussen's near no-hitter in Game 1 ending the team's seven-game postseason losing streak.<sup>[35]</sup> In the Championship Series, they defeated the Cleveland Guardians in six games to advance to the World Series for the first time since 2020 and the third time in franchise history (2008, 2020).<sup>[36]</sup> Yandy Diaz was the only remaining player from the 2020 team.<sup>[e]</sup> The Rays sought their first World Series victory after losing to the Phillies in 2008 and the Dodgers in 2020.

### Game 1

Game 1 of the 2026 World Series was the first World Series game to take place at American Family Field, with the last World Series game in Milwaukee taking place at Milwaukee County Stadium in Game 5 of the 1982 World Series. The Milwaukee Bucks of National Basketball Association moved the time of their home opener to 3 p.m. CT in order to not conflict with Game 1.<sup>[43]</sup> The Brewers named Jacob Misiorowski as their starter for Game 1, with the Rays countering with veteran Nick Martinez.<sup>[44]</sup><sup>[45]</sup> Mickey Guyton performed "The Star-Spangled Banner".<sup>[46]</sup> Longtime Brewers shortstop and Baseball Hall-of-Famer Robin Yount threw out the ceremonial first pitch, with the ceremonial ball being given to Yount by Brewers founder and former MLB commissioner Bud Selig.<sup>[47]</sup>

After Misiorowski induced a double play to get out of a jam in the top of the first inning, the Brewers scored the game's first runs in the bottom of the first inning on a single by Jackson Chourio, a run batted in (RBI) triple by Christian Yelich, and an RBI single by William Contreras. The Rays scored their first run in the top of the fourth inning and cut the deficit in half 2–1, with a walk by Jonathan Aranda, a double by Junior Caminero, and an RBI groundout by Liam Hicks, but left the tying run at third base. Misiorowski pitched five innings, giving up four hits, one run, and striking out three batters. Rays starter Nick Martinez nearly matched him after a rocky first, pitching five innings, giving up five hits, two runs, and striking out five batters.<sup>[42]</sup>

In the bottom of the seventh inning, with Cooper Pratt on second base, Chourio hit an RBI single, extending the Brewers' lead 3–1. The Rays loaded the bases in the ninth inning against Trevor Megill, Milwaukee's closer. Liam Hicks hit a ball that initially was ruled a game-ending double play, but after a Rays challenge, replay showed that Cooper Pratt took his foot off the second base bag before he caught the ball. It was subsequently overturned into an RBI groundout that scored Jorge Mateo, and the game continued. Jonny DeLuca subsequently struck out to end the game, giving Milwaukee the 3–2 win. This was the third time Megill thus far this postseason had put the go-ahead runners on base in the ninth inning, but he escaped each game with the save.<sup>[42]</sup>

Misiorowski's first pitch of the night was measured at 103.5 mph (166.57 km/h), the fastest pitch ever recorded in a World Series game (topping the 103.2 mph (166.08 km/h) pitch by relief pitcher Aroldis Chapman in 2016) as well as the fastest by a World Series starter (the Mets' Noah Syndergaard threw a 101.1 mph (162.70 km/h) pitch in Game 3 of the 2015 Series).<sup>[48]</sup><sup>[f]</sup> The second inning featured the first Automated Ball-Strike (ABS) System challenge in a World Series game; catcher William Contreras successfully challenged a ball that ABS determined to be a strike, resulting in an inning-ending strikeout of Víctor Mesa Jr.<sup>[42]</sup> This was the first World Series Game 1 since 2000 to not feature any home runs.<sup>[49]</sup>

### Game 2

[edit]

Yandy Díaz reached second base on an error by Pratt to open the game, and scored on an RBI single by Chandler Simpson. Simpson stole second base and scored on an RBI single by Caminero. Liam Hicks then hit a two-run home run. In the bottom of the first inning, Chourio and Jake Bauers led off for Milwaukee with singles; Chourio scored on an RBI single by Contreras, and Bauers scored on an RBI single by Garrett Mitchell. Henderson left the game after pitching three innings.<sup>[50]</sup>

In the bottom of the fourth inning, Pratt walked and Sal Frelick singled, with Pratt scoring on a fielding error by Jonathan Aranda on a ground ball by David Hamilton. A walk to Bauers loaded the bases, and Cam Booser relieved Rasmussen, retiring Christian Yelich on a groundout. With Ian Seymour pitching for the Rays in the bottom of the sixth inning, Frelick hit a home run to tie the game at 4–4. Milwaukee took a 5–4 lead in the bottom of the seventh inning when Brice Turang doubled and Pratt hit an RBI single. After a scoreless eighth inning, Jonny DeLuca started the top of the ninth inning with a double off of Aaron Ashby, but was stranded there as the Brewers won the game. Milwaukee's bullpen tossed six scoreless innings after Henderson's exit. It was their seventh come-from-behind win in the 2026 postseason.<sup>[50]</sup>

### Game 3

[edit]

Game 3 of the 2026 World Series marked the second time that World Series games were held at Tropicana Field, and the third game overall, following Game 2 of the 2008 World Series. The Rays' most recent World Series appearance in 2020 took place at Globe Life Field as a neutral venue due to the COVID-19 pandemic, which necessitated a neutral-site bubble.<sup>[55]</sup><sup>[56]</sup> Carly Pearce sang the national anthem<sup>[57]</sup> and former Rays manager Joe Maddon threw out the ceremonial first pitch.<sup>[58]</sup> Freddy Peralta started Game 3 for the Rays, while the Brewers countered with Robert Gasser.<sup>[59]</sup>

Milwaukee scored first in the top of the third inning with a single by Jackson Chourio, a walk by Jake Bauers, and RBI singles by Christian Yelich and William Contreras. The Brewers loaded the bases in the fifth inning, knocking Freddy Peralta out of the game. With Cam Booser pitching, Brice Turang hit a two-RBI single, scoring Chourio and Yelich, followed by an RBI single by Garrett Mitchell, a two-RBI double by Cooper Pratt, and an RBI double by Sal Frelick. Booser left the game without recording an out, and Cole Sulser allowed an RBI single to David Hamilton and an RBI double to Chourio before getting out of the inning, with eight total two-out runs scored by the Brewers, all scored after the Brewers won a replay challenge of a called force-out of Yelich at second base to extend the inning.<sup>[54]</sup> In the fifth inning, the Brewers became the first team to have seven consecutive hits in a postseason game.<sup>[60]</sup>

Gasser pitched six innings, allowing no runs and one hit.<sup>[54]</sup> The Rays scored their only run in the ninth inning on a double by Yandy Díaz off of Brandon Woodruff, the longest tenured Brewers player, who was pitching in his first game since July 4 after recovering from a shoulder injury.<sup>[61]</sup> The nine-run win was the largest World Series blowout since Game 2 of the 2019 World Series.<sup>[62]</sup> At 22 years old, Chourio became the youngest player to record four hits in a World Series game since Joe Garagiola in the 1946 World Series.<sup>[63]</sup> In addition, Milwaukee's eight consecutive postseason wins from Game 4 of the NLDS onward matched the 2019 Nationals, 2014 Royals, 2005 White Sox, and 2004 Red Sox for the most consecutive playoff wins in MLB history.<sup>[64]</sup>

### Game 4

Ne-Yo performed the national anthem, and longtime Rays third baseman Evan Longoria threw the ceremonial first pitch.<sup>[65]</sup> Griffin Jax started Game 4 for Tampa Bay,<sup>[66]</sup> while Dustin May started for Milwaukee.<sup>[67]</sup>

In the bottom of the second inning, Jonny DeLuca scored on an RBI double by Chandler Simpson. The Brewers tied the game in the top of the fourth inning, when Sal Frelick hit a single and Cooper Pratt hit an RBI double. The Rays retook the lead in the bottom of the fourth inning on a fielder's choice by DeLuca that scored Caminero. David Hamilton had attempted to tag Caminero on DeLuca's groundout, missed, and then missed first base on his throw to first. Hamilton tied the game for Milwaukee in the top of the fifth inning with a home run. The game remained tied into extra innings.<sup>[68]</sup>

In the top of the twelfth inning, Pratt hit a home run off Ian Seymour to break the tie, giving the Brewers a 3–2 lead. In the bottom half of the inning, Caminero reached on an error and Liam Hicks singled to get Caminero to third base; Cedric Mullins replaced Caminero as a pinch runner. DeLuca then hit a single to score Mullins and tie the game. Simpson, after an aborted plan to bunt the runners, singled to load the bases, and pinch hitter Ben Williamson hit a single into right field to score pinch runner Nick Fortes. It was the first walk-off win for Tampa Bay in the postseason since Game 4 of the 2020 World Series, which was also their last World Series victory.<sup>[68]</sup> This marked the first World Series walk-off pinch hit since Gene Larkin's Game 7 base hit to win the 1991 World Series for the Minnesota Twins in extra innings.<sup>[69]</sup>

Brewers left-handed reliever Aaron Ashby retired all seven batters he faced in Game 4, breaking Andrew Miller’s record for scoreless innings by a reliever in one postseason.<sup>[70]</sup> Jackson Chourio also recorded two more hits in Game 4, giving him a total of 10 in the first four games of the Series; this tied the World Series record for most hits in the first four games of a Series, set by Babe Ruth in 1928.<sup>[71]</sup>
